items.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

26.924.20706

### What subscription do you have?

Plus

### What platform is your computer?

Linux Mint, X11, amd64

### What issue are you seeing?

After updating from 26.917.71314 to 26.924.20706, every local Codex task hangs indefinitely at "Starting your task".

This reproduces with both an existing project task and a brand-new trivial task.

Troubleshooting performed:
- Fully exited and restarted the desktop app: no change.
- Rebooted the machine: no change.
- Tested with VS Code closed and only one Codex app-server running: no change.
- Confirmed the app-server remains responsive to config/account/thread-list requests.
- Recent logs from the failing build contain no thread/start or turn submission corresponding to the attempted task.
- Logs repeatedly contain:
  "ignoring invalid experimental feature enablement keys: apps_mcp_path_override"
- Downgraded only the ChatGPT/Codex Desktop package from 26.924.20706 to 26.917.71314, preserving ~/.codex and all other local state.
- Tasks immediately began working again.

APT history confirms:
26.917.71314 -> 26.924.20706

The older build's logs show normal thread/start and TurnInput dispatch. The failing build does not appear to dispatch the task to the app-server at all.

Expected:
Submitting a local task should create/start the thread and dispatch the user input.

Actual:
UI remains indefinitely at "Starting your task".

Workaround:
Downgrade to 26.917.71314.

This looks like a regression introduced between 26.917.71314 and 26.924.20706, possibly in the Desktop UI/app-server protocol or task-dispatch path.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Install 26.924.20706 on Linux and try to launch a codex task

### What is the expected behavior?

_No response_

_No response_

items.body:
## What happened to my work

I'm fucking furious. On **September 25, 2026**, I ran Codex on Windows using **GPT-6 Astra on Ultra**. It consumed the approximately **50% of my WEEKLY Codex allowance that I had remaining**, and it did not complete my repair. Not 50% of a five-hour window—half of my weekly allowance, gone in one day without the end-to-end working result I requested.

After my main allowance ran out, the task continued on **GPT-5.6 Luna Light through Luna Reserve**. Luna was trying to rescue the unfinished work. It did not cause the original failure.

My later screenshot shows **7h 15m 27s**, **“Goal usage limited”**, and **“You're out of Codex and Work usage.”** The interface tells me to add credits or wait until **September 30, 2026, 3:14 PM**. My application is still failing in the evidence I supplied. The earlier description that the task was continuing on reserve is no longer the latest captured state.

## My Daybreak participation and blocked security research

**I participate in OpenAI Daybreak / Trusted Access for Cyber and use these tools for authorized security research in my own environment. That material context was omitted from the initial report and emails.** This is not just a complaint about slow app development. These recurring Codex failures are preventing me from carrying out the security research I use Daybreak for.

**How the fuck am I supposed to conduct security research when the tool is constantly broken and consumes my allowance without finishing the repair?**

Security research requires a working execution path and repeatable results. When the tool interrupts work, changes state during failed repair attempts, needs repeated recovery, or exhausts the allowance before validation, I cannot reliably reproduce a finding, distinguish a target defect from a tooling failure, validate a patch, or finish the intended end-to-end test. My time and available usage go into recovering the toolchain instead of conducting research.

I am not claiming that Daybreak caused the HTTP 502 or that the screenshots establish the root cause. **My Daybreak research is the work being blocked.** OpenAI needs to investigate the Codex execution failures and account-level usage alongside the effect on my research, rather than treating this as an isolated local-model inconvenience or a generic explanation of Ultra pricing.

Please include the **Daybreak / Trusted Access team** in the human engineering escalation, alongside the Codex team and account Support. My participation and access history can be correlated privately against my affected account. I am not publishing private program correspondence, research material, or account identifiers here.

I need a functioning research toolchain, preservation of my explicit requirements and authorized local-model permissions, and a complete working test—not another governance layer, another receipt, or a smaller task substituted for the one I asked you to finish.

## My environment

- ChatGPT Pro.
- Codex Desktop on Windows.
- GPT-6 Astra, Ultra, throughout the day's primary work; Luna Reserve afterward when the main allowance was exhausted.
- Daybreak / Trusted Access for Cyber participation and authorized security-research use.
- My exact Codex app/CLI build and affected task ID are not available in these screenshots. Please arrange a private diagnostic handoff rather than asking me to publish private project material.
- The percentages are what I observed in the usage meter. The displayed goal time is elapsed goal time, not a measurement of uninterrupted model compute. Please reconcile the consumption against your server-side records.

## The repair I actually requested

I needed my application to work end to end through the model already loaded in LM Studio. I explicitly required runtime discovery of the actual resident model, preservation of its identity and reported context, and no silent loading, unloading, substitution, or hardcoded replacement model.

Instead, my thread records failed configuration candidates, rollbacks, repeated gateway recovery reports, and the original provider/model-route defect remaining open. Codex's own report says:

> “the gateway transport is healthy again, but the provider-unavailable/model-route defect remains open.”

**Getting a gateway process running again after a failed change is not completing my repair. A health check is not a working conversation. A rollback is not delivery.**

## What my screenshots show

1. **At 6h 59m 53s:** the goal was still active, the original route defect remained open, and Luna Reserve showed **16% remaining** while attempting to finish the work Astra left unfinished.
2. **At 7h 15m 27s:** Codex showed **“Goal usage limited”** and **“You're out of Codex and Work usage.”** It offered more credits or a wait until the reset date, not a completed repair.
3. **In my application afterward:** restart-recovery messages were followed by **“LLM request failed (provider internal error, HTTP 502)”** and a matching provider error beside the composer. My normal chat path was still failing.

These captures document the failed outcome and usage-limit interruption. They do not identify the underlying cause of the 502 by themselves. I need the actual failing request and execution history investigated, not another unsupported assumption about which component is responsible.

I am keeping the full screenshots, account details, support case numbers, and private project information out of this public issue. They belong in a private support/engineering investigation.

## This is a recurring failure in my workflow

This is not one unlucky thread. My recurring experience is hours of execution, partial changes, repeated checking, scope drift, recovery work, and then another unfinished or partially broken application. My apps are not working properly end to end. I keep having to supervise, correct, test, and repair work that Codex was supposed to finish.

I have been building this ecosystem for roughly two years. My recent ChatGPT conversations increasingly consist of complaints about Codex instead of the development work I came here to do. I am tired of seeing one-shot success stories while my own paid workflow burns an entire day and half a week's allowance without delivering the working result.

I am done with governance detours, repeated approval discussions, and mountains of receipts with no finished application. **I am not asking you to solve this by stopping earlier and leaving my system broken, shrinking my request, or telling me to buy another reset.** I need the authorized work completed while preserving existing functionality.

## My unresolved Support experience

I also have an older, separate paid-reset dispute. A September 21 Support reply acknowledged my requested remedy but said the purchase/reset sequence and remaining allowance still needed review. It did not give me the completed reconciliation, a decision, or a deadline. A September 24 automated follow-up then warned that the case would close unless I replied again and that replying after closure would create a new case.

Why am I responsible for keeping the case alive when the outstanding action is the account review Support said it needed to perform?

That older dispute is separate from today's approximately 50% weekly allowance consumed during this failed repair. Do not conflate the incidents or add their percentages together. Please connect my existing support history privately instead of making me restart the complaint each time.

## What I need from OpenAI

1. **One named human owner** coordinating Codex engineering, the Daybreak / Trusted Access team, and account Support, with escalation to Tibo Sottiaux. Give me the next concrete action and a response date. An automated duplicate suggestion is not human help.
2. **A practical recovery path for my unfinished applications and blocked security research.** Preserve my original requirements, authorized local-model permissions, and existing functionality. The acceptance criterion is the requested application and authorized research workflow working end to end, not process health, a completed turn, or a green component test.
3. **Restoration of the approximately 50% weekly allowance consumed during this failed work**, and a separate decision on my older paid-reset claim. This is my service-recovery request, not an assertion that every consumed unit was an accounting error. If maintainers cannot authorize adjustments, hand the request to someone who can.
4. **An actual task-level usage investigation:** model and reasoning effort, subagents, retries, compactions, repeated operations, and automatic reviews. Distinguish useful implementation from failed/repeated work and investigate accounting as well as execution behavior. “Ultra uses more compute” does not explain the absence of a working result.
5. **A concrete explanation of what will prevent recurrence.** A refill alone does not fix a product that burns the next allowance repeating the same failure. Please preserve the relevant session and usage records, and investigate why my research toolchain remains unreliable despite my Daybreak participation.

I am angry, exhausted, and tired of paying to supervise unfinished repairs. **If another day and another chunk of my allowance disappear while Codex leaves my systems broken again, I am quitting ChatGPT.**

Who is taking ownership, what happens next, and when will I receive the investigation results and service-recovery decision?

Related reports: #47566, #47514, #44974, #42080, #42937, #41220. These may help correlate symptoms; I am not asserting that every incident has the same root cause. Please preserve my account-specific incident and recovery request when linking reports.

items.title: Fix zsh alias quoting in sourced shell snapshots
items.body:
Fix zsh alias quoting in sourced shell snapshots

## Why

Sourced snapshots parse options and aliases as a group before restored options take effect. Aliases serialized with `RC_QUOTES` enabled can therefore be misinterpreted by the replay shell.

## What changed

Serialize zsh aliases for sourced snapshots with `NO_RC_QUOTES` in a subshell, preserving the captured shell options and avoiding a dependency on the optional `zsh/parameter` module.

## Testing

Extend regression coverage to execute restored aliases with `RC_QUOTES` enabled and disabled across source and eval replay. Expand macOS zsh concurrent replay tests to cover quoted aliases, preserved options, and blocked descriptor paths with and without a TTY.

labels.name: bug

labels.description: Issues related to tool calling

items.body:
## Environment

- Codex desktop on Windows 10, build19045; the actions were not run from standalone CLI.
- Execution context reports `sandbox_mode=danger-full-access`, `approval_policy=never`,
  `permission_profile=disabled`, network enabled.
- Executable metadata reports ProductName `Codex`, ProductVersion153.0.8010.53.
  The user-facing application release has not been independently verified; these
  metadata may identify the embedded runtime rather than the application release.
- Organization-managed status is unknown. No policy/permission configuration was changed.

## Observed errors (25September2026, Europe/Moscow)

At16:52:45, an authorized browser task returned:

> Browser Use rejected this action due to browser security policy. Reason: The site-safety policy blocks this action; no user permission prompt or Auto-review was attempted. Browser use is not permitted on https://vk.ru/[group].

The response explicitly prohibited indirect execution/workarounds. The action was
not repeated through another surface. This appears to be site-safety, not Auto-review.

At21:29:30, a diagnostic compound PowerShell call returned:

> exec_command failed: CreateProcess { message: Rejected(... rejected: blocked by policy) }

The call searched two local Python sources with `rg`, then requested an Android
ACTION_VIEW of a public Ozon product on an owner-authorized dedicated device:

```text
adb -s [DEVICE] shell am start -a android.intent.action.VIEW -d https://www.ozon.ru/product/[SKU]/ -p ru.ozon.app.android
```

Both placeholders above are deliberate redactions. The entire compound command
was rejected before execution; the diagnostic does not identify the policy rule
or which command component triggered it. No equivalent was used to bypass it.

The user tried `/approve` in the desktop composer and reported no command/list.
The suggested `$CODEX_HOME/.sandbox/sandbox.log` file is absent. This does not
establish which policy layer rejected the process.

## Requested clarification

Please identify the supported diagnostic/reporting path for these two rejection
layers and whether either supports user-visible review in this desktop surface.
If an action is intentionally non-reviewable, a clear reason/category and next
supported step would be helpful. We understand Full Access is not an override of
site-safety or managed policy and are not asking to disable or evade protections.

OpenAI Help Center AI support received the description and contact email, but stated
it could not escalate to a specialist or provide a ticket number and referred us
to in-app Feedback or this public issue tracker. No human review is confirmed.

## Related reports checked

- https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/44881 describes ambiguous browser-denial
  scope and a missing review path. Its comments checked on 25 September contain
  no confirmed maintainer resolution; we have not applied the suggested custom fork.
- https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/48128 reports the same Windows error
  wording and no actionable approval record, in the IDE rather than desktop.
- https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/40060 concerns a `Start-Process` plus
  unrelated-URL classifier. Our rejected call contained no `Start-Process`, so
  that report does not establish our cause or justify retrying a split command.

These may overlap with the missing-diagnostic problem; we are not claiming a
shared root cause or a confirmed fix.

items.body:
Codex CLI 0.157.0 transcribes music playing through my audio interface even after I unplug the microphone.

I'm on Intel macOS with an Antelope Audio Zen Go Synergy Core USB interface. My microphone uses input 1. The macOS input device, "Zen Go Synergy Core Playback", exposes 16 channels at 48 kHz.

To reproduce:

1. Set the Zen Go as the macOS default input and output.
2. Play music through the interface and start Codex voice mode.
3. Unplug the microphone while leaving the music playing.

The [voice capture code](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.157.0/codex-rs/voice-host/src/devices.rs) averages all input channels into mono in `build_input`. A level check showed strong activity on channels 3 and 4, separate from input 1. That suggests a playback or loopback channel is reaching voice mode, though I haven't confirmed the interface's routing.

Please let me select input 1 as the microphone source so the other channels aren't included. Voice settings should also show the selected device and input channel.

labels.name: bug

items.body:
### What version of Codex CLI is running?

`codex-cli 0.145.0` (the local update checker reports 0.157.0 as available)

### What subscription do you have?

N/A — custom Azure OpenAI model provider

### Which model were you using?

`gpt-5.6-sol`, medium reasoning

### What platform is your computer?

Ubuntu 20.04 x86_64, GNOME Terminal; Codex installed globally with npm

### Codex doctor report

`codex doctor --json` returned `overallStatus: ok`. Relevant sanitized fields:

```json
{
  "codexVersion": "0.145.0",
  "overallStatus": "ok",
  "model": "gpt-5.6-sol",
  "modelProvider": "azure",
  "platform": "linux-x86_64",
  "installation": "npm",
  "stateDbIntegrity": "ok",
  "rolloutDbParity": "ok",
  "appServerMode": "ephemeral",
  "responsesWebSocket": false
}
```

### What issue are you seeing?

During a long-running media transcription, the agent spontaneously abandoned the active task and began building an unrelated React application named “Rotero”. The user never requested or mentioned Rotero.

There was no new user message, steering event, task boundary, context compaction, rate-limit event, resume, or relevant tool output before the switch. The last tool output contained only transcription progress.

The unrelated work created a new application directory and eventually caused the active transcription process to terminate before completion.

The local rollout log was audited. Across all locally stored user messages, there was no user prompt containing “Rotero” or the invented interface brief before the incident. The frontend skill was loaded only after the agent had already switched objectives, so it was not the trigger.

No audio transcription or customer content is included in this public report.

### Steps to reproduce the bug

The behavior is intermittent, but the observed sequence was:

1. Use a long-lived Codex CLI thread containing multiple earlier tasks.
2. Ask Codex to transcribe two local media files with an existing local speech-to-text model.
3. Let Codex start a long-running process.
4. Codex repeatedly polls the process using `write_stdin` and `wait`, posting progress updates.
5. After a normal progress result, without any user input, Codex changes objectives and begins an unrelated implementation task.

Exact sanitized timeline:

- 2026-09-25 18:21:43 UTC: task started; one user message requested two transcriptions.
- 2026-09-25 18:27:02 UTC: tool result reported normal progress (`00:06:11`).
- 2026-09-25 18:27:08 UTC: the assistant announced it would inspect an app and implement an interface.
- No event exists between these entries that could authorize or explain the scope change.
- The same turn ID remained active throughout.

Identifiers for private telemetry correlation:

- Session ID: `01a03a9f-357e-7df0-8b8c-599975b9bac7`
- Turn ID: `01a0d9cd-43ff-7de3-9e2e-75e3e2db1044`

### What is the expected behavior?

After a tool wait completes, Codex should continue the active user request. A tool result must not replace the current objective. If the model cannot reliably recover the active objective, it should stop and ask for confirmation before creating unrelated files or abandoning a running process.

The runtime should preserve an explicit task pointer across repeated tool continuations and reject scope-changing mutations unless a new user instruction or an existing plan authorizes them.

### Additional information

This differs from known context-loss reports because there was:

- no context compaction;
- no session resume;
- no rate-limit boundary;
- no subagent handoff;
- no new or steered user message.

Potentially related issues:

- #8310 — resume after rate limit continues on wrong context
- #35935 — context compaction loses task state
- #36934 — long-session context regression

The common symptom is task drift, but this reproduction occurs during an uninterrupted turn consisting of repeated tool waits. The issue has reportedly occurred more than once for the user.

Privacy note: the local session transcript contains confidential meeting material and is intentionally not attached publicly. It can be shared through a private support channel if needed.

items.title: Windows: PreToolUse hook exit code 2 does not block; hook commands run under `pwsh -Command`, which reports exit 1

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

labels.name: hooks
labels.description: Issues related to event hooks

items.body:
### What version of Codex CLI is running?

codex-cli 0.157.0 (also seen on 0.155.1)

### What subscription do you have?

Plus

### Which model were you using?

gpt-6-astra

### What platform is your computer?

Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26200.0 x64

### What terminal emulator and version are you using (if applicable)?

Not applicable: reproduced with non-interactive `codex exec`, started from Git Bash. The shell Codex selects is PowerShell 7.6.6 (`pwsh.exe`, WindowsApps alias).

### Codex doctor report

Not included.

### What issue are you seeing?

On Windows, a `PreToolUse` command hook that exits with code 2 and writes a reason to stderr does not block the shell call. The hook runs, and the command executes anyway. The hooks docs say "You can also use exit code `2` and write the blocking reason to `stderr`."

The hook command appears to be launched as `pwsh.exe -NoProfile -Command "<hook command>"` (this is the hook's parent process command line, captured from inside the hook). With `-Command`, PowerShell exits with 1 when the last native command fails, whatever that command's exit code was, so Codex receives 1 instead of 2:

```
$ pwsh -NoProfile -Command "python -c 'import sys; sys.exit(2)'"; echo $?
1
$ pwsh -NoProfile -Command 'python -c "import sys; sys.exit(2)"; exit $LASTEXITCODE'; echo $?
2
```

The JSON deny (`hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision: "deny"` on stdout, exit 0) does block, and so does appending `; exit $LASTEXITCODE` to the hook command.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. `~/.codex/hooks.json`:

```json
{"hooks": {"PreToolUse": [{"matcher": "^Bash$", "hooks": [{"type": "command", "command": "python C:/path/to/exit2_hook.py", "timeout": 30}]}]}}
```

2. `exit2_hook.py`:

```python
import json, sys
json.load(sys.stdin)
sys.stderr.write("repro: this PreToolUse hook blocks every shell command (exit 2)\n")
sys.exit(2)
```

3. Run:

```
codex exec --ephemeral --json --skip-git-repo-check --dangerously-bypass-hook-trust -s read-only "Run exactly this shell command once, then report whether it ran and its output verbatim: echo HOOK_PROBE_RAN"
```

The hook is invoked (it received the `echo HOOK_PROBE_RAN` payload), and the `command_execution` item still completes with exit code 0 and output `HOOK_PROBE_RAN`.

Same setup, only the hook command changed (0.157.0):

| Hook command | Result |
|---|---|
| `python exit2_hook.py` (exit 2 + stderr) | command runs |
| `python exit2_hook.py; exit $LASTEXITCODE` | blocked: `Command blocked by PreToolUse hook: repro: this PreToolUse hook blocks every shell command (exit 2)` |
| `python json_deny_hook.py` (prints the `permissionDecision: "deny"` JSON, exits 0) | blocked |

On 0.155.1 the same happened with a PowerShell hook (`powershell.exe -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File hook.ps1`, ending in `exit 2`).

### What is the expected behavior?

Exit code 2 from a `PreToolUse` hook blocks the call on Windows, as documented. That would need the hook's own exit code to reach Codex unchanged, for example by appending `; exit $LASTEXITCODE` to the `-Command` string or by not wrapping the hook command in `pwsh -Command`.

### Additional information

Related but different: #27833 (deny not enforced for `apply_patch`), #47810 (hook launch fails when the outer shell is Store/MSIX PowerShell), #38168 (hook commands with embedded quotes under `cmd /C`).

Exit code 2 is the simplest way to write a blocking policy hook, so hooks written that way fail open on Windows without the author noticing.

items.title: [Windows] Cannot submit a second message in Codex after the first turn completes

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

labels.name: app-server
labels.description: Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces

items.body:
## Description

In the Codex interface in the ChatGPT Windows app, I can successfully send the first message in a new conversation and Codex responds normally.

After the first response completes, I can type a second message, but I cannot submit it at all. The second message never gets sent.

This happens consistently and makes multi-turn Codex conversations unusable.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Open Codex in the ChatGPT Windows app.
2. Create a new conversation.
3. Send "Hello 1".
4. Wait until Codex finishes responding.
5. Type "Hello 2".
6. Try to submit the message.

## Expected behavior

"Hello 2" should be submitted and Codex should start the second turn.

## Actual behavior

The first turn works normally.

After it completes, the second message can be typed into the composer, but it cannot be submitted.

The issue reproduces consistently in new conversations.

## Troubleshooting already performed

- Confirmed ChatGPT is updated to the latest version available to me.
- Used Windows "Repair" for the ChatGPT app.
  - This temporarily restored functionality once, but the problem returned immediately on the next follow-up message.
- Completely uninstalled and reinstalled ChatGPT.
- Created a completely fresh local Codex profile by renaming `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Codex` and allowing the app to create a new one.
- Reproduced the issue again with the fresh profile.
- General ChatGPT/API connectivity appears functional.

None of these steps resolved the issue.

## Relevant diagnostic logs

Around the failure, the diagnostic logs contain:

`Received turn/started for unknown conversation`

followed by:

`Received turn/completed for unknown conversation`

The logs also showed a state where a thread was considered streaming without an active runtime.

items.title: Make banked Full resets recurring and predictable for heavy Codex users

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: rate-limits
labels.description: Issues related to rate limits, quotas, and token usage reporting

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

items.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

Codex desktop app on macOS, as part of a long-running real-world project workflow.

### What feature would you like to see?

I would like OpenAI to make **banked Full resets a predictable, recurring part of the Codex usage model**, while preserving the current included allowance and normal reset cycle.

A model that would be especially useful would be:

- keep the existing standard usage allowance and its normal reset;
- add **1–2 banked Full resets per monthly/billing cycle** (or an equivalent recurring mechanism);
- let the user redeem those resets manually when a project has an unusually heavy usage week;
- do not reduce the existing allowance in exchange for those additional resets.

This is not a request for unlimited usage. The goal is to create a small, predictable buffer for users who rely on Codex for sustained project work.

### Why this would help

For long-running and complex projects, Codex usage is naturally bursty. A heavy implementation, debugging, review, or validation phase can consume a weekly allowance much faster than a quieter week. When that happens, the project can be interrupted for several days even though the user is actively depending on Codex as part of a real workflow.

Banked Full resets already demonstrate a very useful product mechanism: they let a user bridge an unusually intensive period without removing rate limits altogether. Making that mechanism predictable rather than only occasional or promotional would substantially improve continuity and planning.

For a heavy user, the ideal experience would be something like **one normal cycle reset plus up to two additional banked Full resets over the broader cycle**. That would preserve the existing safeguards while making Codex much more dependable for serious, continuous work.

This request was developed collaboratively with ChatGPT from my actual Codex usage experience and the interruptions I encounter in a long-running project. That collaboration itself is part of why I value the OpenAI ecosystem: ChatGPT helps me reason about the workflow, while Codex helps me execute it.

Thank you for considering it.

---

## Versão em português

Gostaria de sugerir que a OpenAI transforme as **redefinições completas acumuláveis (banked Full resets)** em uma parte previsível e recorrente do modelo de uso do Codex, preservando integralmente a franquia atual e o ciclo normal de renovação.

Um modelo especialmente útil seria:

- manter a franquia de uso atual e sua renovação normal;
- acrescentar **1–2 redefinições completas acumuláveis por ciclo mensal/de cobrança** (ou mecanismo recorrente equivalente);
- permitir que o usuário utilize essas redefinições manualmente quando um projeto tiver uma semana de uso excepcionalmente intenso;
- não reduzir a franquia existente em troca dessas redefinições adicionais.

Não se trata de solicitar uso ilimitado. A proposta é criar uma pequena margem previsível para usuários que dependem do Codex em projetos contínuos.

Projetos longos e complexos têm consumo naturalmente irregular. Fases intensas de implementação, depuração, revisão ou validação podem consumir a franquia semanal muito mais rapidamente, interrompendo o trabalho por vários dias.

As redefinições completas acumuláveis já demonstram que esse mecanismo funciona muito bem. Torná-lo previsível — em vez de apenas ocasional ou promocional — melhoraria significativamente a continuidade e o planejamento do trabalho.

Para um usuário intensivo, uma experiência ideal seria algo como **uma renovação normal do ciclo mais até duas redefinições completas adicionais ao longo do ciclo mais amplo**, mantendo os limites e salvaguardas já existentes.

Esta sugestão foi desenvolvida em colaboração com o ChatGPT a partir da minha experiência real de uso do Codex e das interrupções que enfrento em um projeto de longo prazo. Essa integração também é parte do valor que encontro no ecossistema da OpenAI: o ChatGPT me ajuda a estruturar e raciocinar sobre o trabalho, enquanto o Codex me ajuda a executá-lo.

Obrigado por considerarem a sugestão.

items.title: Preserve usage limit windows in turn and compaction analytics
items.body:
Preserve usage limit windows in turn and compaction analytics

## Why

Usage limit errors discarded the server-selected window responsible for the limit, leaving turn and compaction analytics unable to distinguish five-hour limits from weekly limits.

## What changed

Preserve optional `limit_window_minutes` from usage limit error responses in `UsageLimitReachedError` and report it as `usage_limit_window_minutes` in turn and compaction events. Accept unsigned integers that fit in `u16`; treat missing, null, malformed, or out-of-range values as unknown. Events for other error kinds report `null`.

## Testing

Add coverage for HTTP and wrapped WebSocket error mapping, analytics serialization and reduction, and app-server propagation to turn and local/remote compaction events. Cases include five-hour and weekly windows, missing or invalid values, and unrelated errors.

items.body:
Subject: Mobile timeout notification opens chat with history but without desktop execution context; assistant misdiagnoses missing capabilities

Affected surfaces: Codex desktop, ChatGPT mobile notifications, and a nested hosted ChatGPT agent.

Codex/app versions at incident: not captured.
Subscription: omitted for privacy.
Platform: macOS desktop; phone OS/version not confirmed.
Frequency: one observed incident; not yet reproduced.

Summary
A user started a task in the Codex desktop app with a local repository/worktree and interactive browser access. During testing of a custom hosted ChatGPT agent connected to an MCP service, a cancellation attempt stalled. The user received a timeout notification in the ChatGPT phone app. Tapping it opened a conversation containing the relevant prior history, but the continuation apparently did not control or reconnect to the original laptop-backed task. The assistant could not access the worktree or the prior execution route, yet initially treated historical tool activity as if it described its own current capabilities.

Reported reproduction sequence (one observed incident; reproducibility not yet established)
1. Start a local task in Codex desktop with a worktree and browser tools.
2. Use browser automation to exercise a hosted ChatGPT agent connected to a custom MCP service.
3. A hosted-agent cancellation/approval attempt stalls; a timeout notification arrives in ChatGPT mobile.
4. Tap the notification and ask the opened conversation to retry or perform a read-only check.
5. Relevant history is visible, but the assistant reports it lacks the local worktree, interactive browser and/or previous agent invocation capability.
6. Only after repeated user corrections and an explicit question about remote control of the laptop does the assistant recognize a possible execution-context mismatch.

Actual behavior and impact
- The notification and preserved history led the user to expect continuation of the original remote desktop task.
- The user reports no clear warning that the opened conversation had a different execution environment, or that it might be a nested hosted-agent conversation rather than the originating Codex task.
- The assistant repeatedly searched its direct connector/tool registry and described the absent entries as a lost MCP/agent capability, without establishing the original access path.
- It claimed to have checked connectivity when it had only checked tool availability, then retracted that claim.
- It promised repository investigation before acknowledging there was no repository mounted in that runtime.
- The user had to diagnose the cross-context distinction; this caused substantial confusion and wasted time.
- Cancellation later succeeded through a separate fresh hosted-agent run. The earlier timeout notification did not describe the final state of the underlying operation.

Short de-identified excerpts from the supplied transcript
User: "I started this session in my laptop. Which has access to my worktree. It seems I'm not interacting remotely to it."
Assistant: "The conversation history synchronized ... but the execution environment/tool attachments did not follow the conversation to this runtime."
User: "I opened this because I had a notification so I assumed it was remote."
These assistant explanations are included as evidence of the conversation, not proof of the internal routing mechanism.

Expected behavior
- Route the notification to the correct originating task and execution environment when remote continuation is supported.
- If it instead opens a nested hosted-agent chat or a cloud-only continuation, clearly label the destination and unavailable desktop capabilities before the user continues.
- Give the assistant reliable provenance: current host/environment, source task versus child agent, live capabilities, and whether earlier tool results came from a different runtime.
- The assistant should immediately distinguish historical context from current access, avoid unsupported claims that an MCP went offline or a dispatcher disappeared, and offer an accurate route back to the original task.
- Timeout notifications should identify the specific attempt and, where possible, surface a later successful outcome rather than implying the underlying operation is still pending.

Evidence and limits
The report is based on the user's account, a supplied conversation export, and desktop-side observations of browser-mediated hosted-agent testing and subsequent successful cleanup. The original notification payload, deep-link target, exact phone app version/OS, and OpenAI routing logs were not captured. Please investigate whether this was incorrect deep-link routing, an intentional but unlabeled context boundary, or another handoff issue. No claim is made that backend MCP availability actually failed or that a direct agent-dispatch tool was removed.

Privacy
Personal names, organization names, account details, internal system/agent names, booking references, room/location names, repository paths/URLs, agent/task/workspace IDs, credentials and raw internal logs are omitted. Please do not publish or forward an unsanitized conversation. This report contains only the minimum generic workflow needed to investigate.

items.title: Feature request: bounded model-side retrieval skill for historical/context search

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: skills
labels.description: Issues related to skills

items.body:
### What feature would you like to see?

A small reusable **model-facing retrieval skill** for historical/context search: a bounded query and verification discipline the model can apply when it has access to an opaque retrieval surface but does not know that surface's ranking or failure modes.

This is not a request for a new memory backend and not a request to expose private retrieval internals.

The simplest useful first pass is:

```text
1. literal / exact-name probe
2. functional rephrase that omits the headline term
3. distinctive relation / phrase probe
```

Escalate only when needed. A fuller bounded pass can add:

```text
semantic
relational / authority
temporal
correction
falsifier
epistemic-boundary
source
```

The skill should preserve distinctions such as:

```text
search miss != historical absence
semantic-region hit != exact entity/reference identification
repeated retrieval of one fragment != independent corroboration
retrieved historical context != current authority
recovering an attractor != recovering its later corrections and limits
```

If materially different formulations keep returning the same fragment without new provenance, stop probing rather than treating repetition as stronger evidence.

### Why

Opaque retrieval often fails in ways that are more subtle than "found" or "not found".

In one live reconstruction case, broad/default retrieval localized the correct semantic area for an older heartbeat/liveness discussion but attached the wrong concrete repository/issue reference. Independent repository readback found the exact historical source elsewhere:

```text
SEMANTIC_REGION = GOOD
ENTITY_LOCALIZATION = WRONG
```

That should be treated as partial retrieval success plus failed locator verification, not as a fully correct answer.

A separate calibrated case showed that functional and relational probes could recover a known historical target even when the query omitted its headline entity name. Controlled reformulation can therefore improve recall without making assumptions about the hidden backend.

### Method lineage

This proposal is not an ad-hoc prompt recipe. It condenses an existing Sonar research line preserved in public Theseus work:

```text
historical semantic-echolocation discipline
-> controlled multi-probe retrieval
-> calibration against independently inspectable Session Search targets
-> literal / semantic / functional / relational / negative-control probes
-> correction / falsifier / epistemic-boundary probes
```

The historical protocol already required several controlled formulations, at least one functional/semantic probe that did not repeat the planted canary name, explicit source/conflict/gap recording, and `UNKNOWN` on retrieval failure rather than absence.

Calibration was then performed against known historical episodes indexed from a **user-owned ChatGPT conversation corpus derived from an official OpenAI account-export ZIP**. That export is conservatively treated as a partial historical snapshot rather than proof of complete or current account history.

The important result is methodological: a model can use controlled probes to recover not only a vivid semantic attractor, but also corrections, counterexamples, epistemic limits, and temporal drift around it.

### Smallest useful implementation

This could initially ship as system guidance or a built-in reusable skill rather than a new API.

Useful behavior:

- use several bounded, materially different probes when historical continuity matters;
- preserve provenance, conflicts, temporal drift, and uncertainty;
- distinguish recurrence from corroboration;
- treat misses conservatively;
- verify exact external references when the final claim depends on them;
- stop when additional probes stop adding new provenance.

A useful diagnostic record can include:

```text
SOURCE
MATCH_TYPE
PROVENANCE
RECURRENCE
CONFLICTS
TEMPORAL_DRIFT
GAPS
CONFIDENCE
```

### Relationship to existing requests

This complements, rather than duplicates:

- #44345 — account-wide / cross-Project search and read-only assistant access;
- #28193 — exact current/past transcript access and search/list helpers;
- #39485 — concrete case where prior-chat retrieval can fail while the assistant may still claim it found/read the conversation.

Those issues are mainly about **having the retrieval surface**. This request is about **how the model should use an available retrieval surface deliberately and verify what it got back**.

### Non-goals

- no reverse engineering of private OpenAI retrieval infrastructure;
- no claim that one retrieval backend is stable across every ChatGPT/Codex runtime;
- no requirement to run multiple probes for ordinary low-stakes queries;
- no replacement for Memory;
- no promotion of retrieved historical material into current authority.

### Public evidence

Research/evidence container:
https://github.com/TeaShaman-cyber/theseus-research/issues/81

Calibrated retrieval methodology:
https://github.com/TeaShaman-cyber/theseus-research/issues/11

Session Search prototype:
https://github.com/TeaShaman-cyber/theseus-session-search-lab

A separate public implementation repository will be used to prototype the skill independently of this feature request.

items.body:
## Summary

On Windows Codex Desktop, the primary runtime selection changes from `26.923.10815` to `26.905.11957`. Both versions install successfully, but the older one remains installed and `load_workspace_dependencies` keeps returning `26.905.11957`.

## Environment

- Windows x64, OS build 10.0.26200
- Microsoft Store package: `OpenAI.Codex 26.917.9434.0`
- Desktop log build number: `10954`
- Runtime source: `archive`, release: `latest`, config source: `statsig-layer`

## Evidence (2026-09-25 UTC, sanitized)

- `13:49:50.906`: `Codex runtime config selected` with `latest.bundleVersion=26.923.10815`, `source=statsig-layer`.
- `13:49:50.947`: installer selects the `26.923.10815` win32-x64 archive.
- `13:49:56.715`: `Statsig: error while bootstrapping post-login client`, `Timed out while fetching post-login Statsig bootstrap`.
- `13:50:00.778`: another `Codex runtime config selected` event in the same desktop process has `latest.bundleVersion=26.905.11957`, also `source=statsig-layer`.
- `13:56:11.385`: installer reports `bundleVersion=26.923.10815 outcome=installed`.
- `14:00:40.984`: a subsequent desktop process selects `latest.bundleVersion=26.905.11957`.
- `14:10:13.620`: installer reports `bundleVersion=26.905.11957 outcome=installed`.
- Current `runtime.json` and `load_workspace_dependencies` both report `26.905.11957`.

There is no checksum or installation failure in these two successful install outcomes. The logs do not establish whether the change is an intentional rollout/rollback or a stale configuration after Statsig bootstrap timeout.

## Expected behavior

The Desktop should select a consistent authoritative `latest` runtime for this client/account, or explain an intentional rollback. An already installed newer runtime should not be replaced by an older `latest` value unexpectedly.

## Questions

1. Is `26.905.11957` intentionally selected for this cohort despite `26.923.10815` being selected moments earlier?
2. Can a Statsig bootstrap timeout cause the runtime layer to revert to an older cached `latest`?
3. Is there a supported way to refresh the runtime selection without repeatedly reinstalling bundles?

Related: #46177 (runtime version mismatch, but that report also involved an external startup updater). This case was observed in the Desktop's own startup and install logs. I can provide full logs privately if needed; they are not attached here because they may contain local identifiers.

items.body: ### What issue are you seeing? On Windows, the ChatGPT/Codex Chrome extension can open and continue existing Codex chats normally, but it cannot create a brand-new chat. When I start a new chat in the Chrome extension and send the first message, the extension immediately displays: > Error creating chat > The system cannot find the file specified. > (os error 2) The failure appears specific to creation of a new/root conversation. Existing conversations work normally through the same Chrome extension. **Environment** - Codex app version: 26.917.71314 - Windows MSIX package: OpenAI.Codex_26.917.9434.0_x64 - Codex CLI used by the Chrome integration: 0.155.0-alpha.16.4 - Platform: Windows x64 - Browser: Google Chrome - Authentication: ChatGPT account ### What steps can reproduce the bug? 1. Open the ChatGPT/Codex Chrome extension. 2. Start a completely new chat. 3. Enter any message, for example `hello`. 4. Send the message. 5. The new conversation is not created. 6. The extension displays: `Error creating chat — The system cannot find the file specified. (os error 2)` Control test: 1. Create a brand-new conversation in the Codex Desktop app. 2. Send the first message from Desktop. This works normally. 3. Leave/close that conversation in Desktop so its ownership lock is released. 4. Open that same conversation from the Chrome extension. 5. Send another message from Chrome. 6. The message sends successfully and receives a normal response. Therefore, the Chrome extension can discover, open, and continue existing conversations; the failure occurs specifically when the Chrome extension attempts to create the conversation itself. ### What is the expected behavior? Starting a new chat from the Chrome extension should create a new Codex conversation and submit the first message normally, just as creating a new conversation from the Codex Desktop app does. The Chrome extension should support both creating new conversations and continuing existing conversations. ### Additional information I performed extensive diagnostics to distinguish this from a general Chrome/native-host/runtime failure. **What works** - Codex Desktop can create new conversations normally. - The Codex Desktop built-in browser works normally. - The Chrome extension can list and open existing conversations. - After the Desktop conversation lock is released, the Chrome extension can send new messages to an existing conversation and receive responses normally. **Chrome/native-host checks** - The Chrome NativeMessagingHosts registry entry exists and is valid. - The registered `com.openai.codexextension` manifest exists. - The manifest points to an existing `extension-host.exe`. - Chrome successfully launches `extension-host.exe`. **App-server registration** - The generated `chrome-native-hosts-v2.json` files initially contained stale historical runtime registrations from previous Codex versions. - I backed up and removed only those generated manifests and allowed Codex to regenerate them. - The regenerated manifest contains only the current runtime: AppVersion: 26.917.71314 NodeOK: True ResourcesOK: True HostOK: True - The new-chat error remained unchanged after rebuilding this state. **Chrome plugin app-server runtime** The following binaries in `~\.codex\plugins\.plugin-appserver\` were compared with the currently working Codex Desktop runtime: - `codex.exe` - `codex-code-mode-host.exe` - `codex-command-runner.exe` - `codex-windows-sandbox-setup.exe` All four exist and are byte-identical to the working Desktop copies by SHA-256. The exact Chrome-side Codex executable also runs successfully: codex-cli 0.155.0-alpha.16.4 Exit code: 0 and: codex app-server --help Exit code: 0 There are no `CODEX_CLI_PATH` overrides at the process, user, or machine level. I also tested with a newly generated `config.toml`; the problem was unchanged, so I restored my original configuration. **Current workaround** Creating the conversation in Codex Desktop first, releasing it there, and then opening it in Chrome works. Once the conversation already exists, Chrome can continue it normally. This appears to isolate the failure to the Chrome extension's new/root conversation creation path rather than general native messaging, authentication, app-server startup, or existing-thread operation.

> Experimental feature request failed

`codex doctor --all --json` reports that the background server is running and that both the CLI and app-server are version 0.157.0.

```bash

codex
```

and says that restarting cannot resolve the compatibility check.

codex features disable workspace_dependencies

app-server: 0.157.0
background server status: running
daemon_auto_start: enabled
workspace_dependencies: enabled

install: Homebrew, macOS Apple Silicon

items.title: Fix Guardian retained context spacing and empty assistant handling
items.body:
Fix Guardian retained context spacing and empty assistant handling

## Why

Complete assistant messages with empty text can produce misleading omitted-context notices in Guardian reviews.

## What changed

- Skip complete, empty assistant messages when recording and rendering retained context, while preserving omission notices for incomplete messages.
- Separate retained instruction fragments with blank lines and keep blank lines free of role prefixes, while labeling every nonempty line with its original role.
- Update source-order guidance detection and empty-section deduplication for the added spacing.

## Testing

Extend retained-context tests to cover empty completed messages across resume, restored empty messages, incomplete-message notices, blank-line spacing, and role labeling. Update Guardian prompt snapshots.

items.title: Allow Windows daemon launches with residual job membership
items.body:
Allow Windows daemon launches with residual job membership

## Why

A Windows breakaway launch can leave an outer Job Object attached after escaping an inner job. Job membership alone does not establish whether the daemon will be terminated, so rejecting all remaining membership can block valid launches.

## What changed

Remove the job-membership checks from the launch preflight and the spawned daemon. Keep the suspended breakaway probe to verify that launch is permitted before stopping an existing daemon, and terminate and reap the probe afterward.

## Testing

Add a Windows regression test with nested jobs that verifies the probe and daemon leave the inner job while retaining the outer job, and that daemon startup succeeds.

items.title: Preserve filesystem denials when preparing approved commands
items.body:
Preserve filesystem denials when preparing approved commands

## Why

Approved commands need broader write access while retaining explicit read denials. On Linux, binding the filesystem root writable can shadow standard devices, and additional root-metadata mounts can reopen denied symlink targets.

## What changed

- Add `FileSystemSandboxPolicy::for_approved_command` to grant root and root-metadata writes while retaining path and glob denials. Keep the original policy when denials cannot be resolved or deny the root.
- Restore standard devices after Linux writable root binds, then apply explicit deny masks. Avoid redundant root-alias binds and inherit root-metadata writes from the root mount so denied targets stay masked.
- Preserve literal deny paths alongside resolved targets so Linux can reject denials that cross writable symlinks.
- Advertise Linux device and approved-root restriction support through two opt-in exec-server capabilities, omitted from serialization when false.

## Testing

Add regression coverage for approval policy materialization across Unix, Windows drive, and UNC paths; Windows volume expansion; Linux device access and metadata symlink restrictions; and capability serialization compatibility.

## Summary
In Codex desktop on Windows, Gmail tools appeared in the tool catalogue after a reset, but could not be invoked through the execution runtime. Support recommended filing a GitHub issue and including the in-app Feedback IDs below so uploaded log bundles can be correlated.

## Feedback IDs
- Original: `01a0d88a-6f14-7fa3-81d1-454f2b3bd364`
- Additional diagnostic evidence: `01a0d9b6-04e7-72f1-a80f-cb9902d07826`

## Observed behavior
1. Gmail tools appeared in the initial tool catalogue.
2. Runtime inspection returned `undefined` for `tools.mcp__codex_apps__gmail_get_profile` and `tools.mcp__codex_apps__gmail_list_labels`.
3. Invoking the profile function returned:
   `TypeError: tools.mcp__codex_apps__gmail_get_profile is not a function`
4. Invoking `gmail_list_labels` also returned a matching TypeError.
5. These invocations failed locally before connector dispatch or Gmail authentication.
6. The exact `gmail_get_profile` entry was absent during inspection; `gmail_list_labels` was initially advertised but absent from a later catalogue check.

## Related previously reported failure
The original support investigation reported `codex_apps` failing MCP `initialize` with `error decoding response body` and status `failed`. That earlier log was not independently inspected during the runtime reproduction above. Please correlate the uploaded logs to determine whether initialization failure caused the catalogue/runtime mismatch.

## Expected behavior
Advertised tools should have callable runtime bindings once ready, or the client should clearly surface the server initialization/unavailable state instead of exposing an unusable tool.

## Environment and limitations
- Codex desktop on Windows.
- Exact app version/build not captured in this reproduction; please consult the feedback bundles.
- Interactive `/mcp` output was not available to the assistant and is not attached here.
- `mcp_optional_startup_grace_ms = 0` was suggested as an optional diagnostic but has not been applied or tested in this investigation.
- No claim is made that Gmail credentials are invalid, or that changing startup timing would fix the response-decoding error.

items.title: Add item anchors to `thread/items/list` pagination
items.body:
Add item anchors to `thread/items/list` pagination

## What changed

Allow `cursor` to accept an item anchor such as `{"type":"item","itemId":"item-123"}` with a non-empty `turnId`. Ascending pagination returns items after the anchor; descending pagination returns items before it. The anchor itself is excluded, and subsequent pages use the returned opaque string cursor.

Resolve anchors within the requested turn's visible history, including inherited fork history. Reject missing turn IDs and empty, unknown, or out-of-scope item IDs with invalid params (`-32602`). Preserve existing string and null cursor behavior, and update the protocol schemas, TypeScript and Python types, and API documentation.

## Testing

Add protocol round-trip and invalid-shape tests, app-server coverage for anchored pagination and errors, and thread-store coverage for growing turns, reverse pagination, page boundaries, fork visibility, and anchor scope validation.

items.title: Agent role enabled = false does not disable an existing parent MCP server

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: mcp
labels.description: Issues related to the use of model context protocol (MCP) servers

labels.name: subagent
labels.description: Issues involving subagents or multi-agent features

labels.name: config
labels.description: Issues involving config.toml, config keys, config merging, or config updates

items.body:
## Summary

A custom agent role may parse a valid mcp_servers entry with enabled = false, but applying the role leaves the effective parent MCP server enabled.

## Minimal configuration

Parent configuration:

[mcp_servers.demo]
command = "demo-command"

Custom role file:

[mcp_servers.demo]
command = "demo-command"
enabled = false

The command is a config-only test fixture and is never started. It is included because a standalone role MCP entry must have a valid transport.

The expected result is that the existing demo server remains configured but has enabled == false. A role must still not be able to add a server that the parent did not configure.

## Source findings

At commit 1bf73324cadc72a53ed467edc7d3fd2b145a6166:

AgentRoleOverrides whitelists scalar, feature, and skill overrides but omits MCP servers.

Role parsing/deserialization occurs before that projection at role.rs#L79-L126, so the role file is valid but its MCP configuration is discarded.

build_next_config clones the effective config and applies the whitelist; it does not update mcp_servers.

The existing anti-authority test at role_tests.rs#L433-L525 intentionally verifies that a role cannot introduce an attacker MCP server. That invariant should remain.

## Regression test

Add this test beside the existing role tests:

#[tokio::test]
async fn apply_role_disables_existing_mcp_server() {
    let (home, mut config) = test_config_with_cli_overrides(vec![(
        "mcp_servers.demo.command".to_string(),
        TomlValue::String("demo-command".to_string()),
    )])
    .await;
    let role_path = write_role_config(
        &home,
        "disabled-mcp-role.toml",
        r#"
[mcp_servers.demo]
command = "demo-command"
enabled = false
"#,
    )
    .await;
    config.agent_roles.insert(
        "custom".to_string(),
        AgentRoleConfig {
            description: None,
            config_file: Some(role_path),
            nickname_candidates: None,
        },
    );

    apply_role_to_config(&mut config, Some("custom"))
        .await
        .expect("custom role should apply");

    assert!(
        !config
            .mcp_servers
            .get()
            .get("demo")
            .expect("parent MCP server should remain configured")
            .enabled
    );
}

From codex-rs, its focused command is:

just test -p codex-core apply_role_disables_existing_mcp_server

This is an expected failing regression on the cited revision, based on the source flow above. It was not executed: this checkout has neither just nor rustfmt, and no toolchain installation or cold build was performed for this issue-only investigation.

## Related issues

#20135 discusses empty-map semantics; this report concerns disabling an already configured named server.
#31097 concerns role selection; it does not appear to cover applying a role-local MCP disable override.

## Documentation

The role file shape is documented in the custom agent file schema.

items.title: Windows app hangs on splash screen and becomes Not Responding on Windows build 26200

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

items.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

26.917.9434.0

### What subscription do you have?

ChatGPT Business

### What platform is your computer?

Windows 11 x64, OS build 10.0.26200

### What issue are you seeing?

### What version of the Codex App are you using?

OpenAI.Codex 26.917.9434.0
Package:
OpenAI.Codex_26.917.9434.0_x64__2p2nqsd0c76g0

### What platform is your computer?

Windows 11 x64
OS version reported by Codex log: 10.0.26200

### What issue are you seeing?

The ChatGPT/Codex Windows desktop app consistently hangs during startup.

The window appears and reaches the OpenAI/ChatGPT splash screen with the logo in the centre, but then becomes unresponsive. Windows shows "ChatGPT (Not Responding)".

Task Manager shows multiple Codex/ChatGPT child processes still running. The main ChatGPT process typically consumes several hundred MB of RAM and remains stuck indefinitely.

The web version of ChatGPT works normally.

### Relevant startup log

The application backend appears to start successfully.

The log reaches:

windows_core_runtime_launch_selected architecture=x64
Launching app
AppServerConnection Starting app-server connection
stdio_transport_spawned
window ready-to-show
window main frame finished load
initialize_handshake_result outcome=success
Codex CLI initialized
app_server_connection.state_changed ... next=connected
Host startup critical-path phases completed

The renderer also logs:

[electron-message-handler] [statsig-refresh-diagnostics] React root render requested

The app then remains frozen on the splash screen.

There is also this warning:

Failed to start the Artifact Session host:
"Artifact Session host Unix-socket transport is not available on Windows."

However, startup continues successfully after that warning.

There is also:

refresh_local_remote_control_client_id_failed
"Sign in to ChatGPT to check remote control authorization."

The app-server and Codex CLI had already successfully initialized before this.

### Troubleshooting already performed

- Ended all ChatGPT/Codex processes in Task Manager
- Rebooted Windows multiple times
- Windows App Repair
- Windows App Reset
- Uninstalled and reinstalled ChatGPT/Codex
- Launched immediately after a clean reboot
- Tested launch with --disable-gpu
- Renamed ~/.codex/auth.json to force fresh authentication
- Renamed/cleared local Codex runtime/state locations
- Renamed LocalCache for the OpenAI.Codex package
- Temporarily disconnected non-essential USB/HID devices
- Closed SimHub, Simucube Tuner, iRacingManager and similar utilities
- Checked Windows Application event log for Application Hang/Application Error events
- Checked System event log for Display, DWM, nvlddmkm and WHEA errors

None of these changed the behaviour.

There were no Display/DWM/NVIDIA/WHEA errors around the failed launches.

### Additional observations

The app consistently creates the window and initializes the local app-server successfully before the UI freezes.

This appears similar to other Windows 26200 reports where background processes start successfully but the desktop UI does not become usable.

The issue persists after reinstall/reset, suggesting it may be a renderer/UI regression rather than corrupted installation state.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Start Windows normally.
2. Launch the ChatGPT/Codex desktop app.
3. The application window opens and shows the OpenAI/ChatGPT splash screen.
4. The splash screen remains visible and the UI never finishes loading.
5. After a short time, Windows marks the application as "Not Responding".
6. Task Manager shows multiple Codex/ChatGPT child processes still running while the main ChatGPT process remains hung.

The issue reproduces consistently after reboot, reinstall, reset, and with non-essential USB/HID devices disconnected.

### What is the expected behavior?

The ChatGPT/Codex desktop app should complete startup after the splash screen and display the normal application UI, allowing me to sign in and use ChatGPT/Codex normally.

### Additional information

The issue still reproduces after extensive troubleshooting.

Notably, the Codex backend appears to start successfully before the UI becomes unresponsive. Logs show the app-server connection succeeds, the main window reaches "ready-to-show", the main frame finishes loading, the Codex CLI initializes successfully, and the connection reaches "connected".

The failure appears to occur after the window/renderer starts, while the splash screen remains visible.

No related Display, DWM, NVIDIA, WHEA, or standard Application Hang errors were found in Windows Event Viewer during the failed launches.

The issue also persists after:
- Windows app Repair and Reset
- uninstall/reinstall
- multiple reboots
- --disable-gpu
- fresh auth state
- fresh Codex local/cache state
- disconnecting non-essential USB/HID devices
- closing SimHub, Simucube, iRacingManager, and similar utilities

The web version works normally.

items.title: Experiment: durable work identity independent of thread lifecycle

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: subagent
labels.description: Issues involving subagents or multi-agent features

labels.name: session
labels.description: Issues involving session (thread) management, resuming, forking, naming, archiving

items.body:
## Summary

I have been testing a downstream Codex runtime where the logical unit of production work is durable independently of the Codex thread that is currently reasoning about it.

The experiment is intentionally narrow:

```text
Thread = one cognition execution
Work   = durable production identity
```

This is **not** a request to merge the downstream runtime into Codex. I am trying to understand whether Codex intends `Thread` / thread-scoped `Goal` to remain the canonical identity for long-running work, or whether a generic work/task identity independent of a cognition thread would be useful as an extension/runtime primitive.

Observed upstream while preparing this issue:

- `openai/codex` main: `c7e80f873f67dbef58206b9d4f3c60e9d556eb16`
- thread goals are durable, but their persisted record is still thread-scoped (`thread_id` is the primary key)
- Codex already exposes useful extension seams such as `ThreadLifecycleContributor`, `TurnLifecycleContributor`, `ToolLifecycleContributor`, extension-private stores, projects, goals, and persisted agent topology

## Why I tested this

For multi-agent or long-running production workflows, the logical task may need to survive:

- thread completion or replacement
- process restart
- model replacement
- child-agent completion
- a later thread continuing the same unfinished objective

A thread can persist and resume, but that is not always the same semantic requirement as saying that the *work itself* has an identity independent of whichever thread/model is currently attached to it.

The concrete question I wanted to test was:

> Can Codex cognition remain transient while production work identity survives independently and is rebound to later threads?

## Downstream experiment

Reference implementation:

- repo: https://github.com/4LFR3Dv1/brinecdx
- tested line: `bcdx/r3-workgraph`
- pinned witness commit: `b649a01834dfeca79e54afbb08f5108121a0b7f2`

Relevant implementation:

- runtime model:
  https://github.com/4LFR3Dv1/brinecdx/blob/b649a01834dfeca79e54afbb08f5108121a0b7f2/codex-rs/brine-runtime/src/model.rs
- durable authority:
  https://github.com/4LFR3Dv1/brinecdx/blob/b649a01834dfeca79e54afbb08f5108121a0b7f2/codex-rs/brine-runtime/src/authority.rs
- Codex lifecycle adapter:
  https://github.com/4LFR3Dv1/brinecdx/blob/b649a01834dfeca79e54afbb08f5108121a0b7f2/codex-rs/ext/brine-runtime/src/lib.rs
- deterministic R3 witness:
  https://github.com/4LFR3Dv1/brinecdx/blob/b649a01834dfeca79e54afbb08f5108121a0b7f2/scripts/witness-r3-workgraph.ps1

The runtime keeps a separate identity:

```text
WorkspaceId
WorkId
SessionId
```

with a record approximately shaped as:

```text
WorkRecord {
    id
    workspace_id
    parent_work
    objective
    status
    assigned_thread
    candidate
    created_revision
    last_revision
}
```

The Codex-facing adapter uses normal extension lifecycle contributors. It does not replace the model loop, TUI, shell semantics, compaction, or ordinary tools.

At thread start/resume, a temporary Codex thread is attached/reconciled to durable work. At thread stop, the thread detaches without deleting the work identity.

## Witness

The R3 witness exercises this sequence against the real runtime implementation:

```text
root session
  -> root Work W1

child session
  -> child Work W2
  -> parent_work = W1

complete child
  -> W2.status = complete

detach child
stop runtime process
restart runtime process

reattach child session
  -> same WorkspaceId
  -> same WorkId W2
  -> same completed Work state
```

It also verifies that the child receives a distinct Work identity instead of reusing the root Work.

The important property is that destroying/replacing the temporary cognition attachment does not destroy the production identity.

## Relationship to existing Codex primitives

I do not think this necessarily implies that Codex needs a new first-class public `Work` type.

Current primitives already cover large parts of the problem:

- persisted threads provide durable conversation/execution history
- thread goals provide durable objective/status state for a thread
- projects provide a higher-level grouping identity
- persisted agent topology tracks parent/child thread relationships
- extension-private state can maintain additional runtime data

The missing distinction in this experiment is specifically:

```text
one logical piece of work
    !=
one thread that is currently executing cognition for it
```

For example, a later thread can attach to the same `WorkId` without requiring the original thread to remain the identity of that work.

## Questions for maintainers

1. Is the intended Codex model that long-running work should remain identified by a durable Thread (with Goal/Project metadata), even when cognition is replaced?

2. If an extension/runtime needs a task identity that can survive and be rebound across multiple threads, is extension-private durable state the intended solution?

3. Is there an existing or planned generic binding surface that an extension should use for something conceptually like:

```text
thread A -> work X
thread B -> work X
child C  -> work Y (parent X)
```

4. If this distinction is useful upstream, would you prefer it to appear as:
   - a generic durable task/work identity,
   - a Goal evolution that is no longer strictly thread-owned,
   - a Project/task relationship,
   - or only a small extension API seam for binding external durable identities to threads?

## Why I am asking before proposing a specific API

The downstream implementation proves the semantics, but it does not prove that its data model is the right Codex abstraction.

I would rather keep the Brine-specific graph downstream and extract only the smallest generic primitive that matches Codex's architecture.

If the intended answer is “keep this entirely extension-private,” that is also useful: it means the existing lifecycle API is already sufficient and the downstream should avoid asking Codex core to own this concept.

## Potential acceptance property, if Codex does want a generic primitive

A minimal generic primitive should make it possible to demonstrate:

```text
create/bind logical work
attach thread A
stop thread A
start thread B
attach thread B to the same logical work
preserve parent/child work lineage
preserve work status across process restart
```

without requiring transcript replay to reconstruct the work identity, and without changing normal Codex behavior when the primitive is unused.

## Non-goals

- replacing Codex Thread/Turn semantics
- replacing Goals or Projects
- changing the model loop
- changing compaction
- changing shell/tool execution
- proposing Brine-specific types for upstream
- requiring a remote runtime for normal Codex use

The downstream exists mainly as executable evidence for the architectural question above.

items.title: Preserve executor MCP credential boundaries across reconnects
items.body:
Preserve executor MCP credential boundaries across reconnects

## Why

Cached executor MCP declarations must not gain access to host environment credentials when reconnecting to an executor that lacks environment credential resolution.

## What changed

- Retain credential policy through MCP registration, catalog materialization, and runtime setup. Derive selected HTTP plugin policy from the plugin's source environment.
- Reject host bearer-token fallback and transports requiring host environment headers or helpers for executor-owned declarations. Preserve host-configured credential resolution.
- Include credential policy in connection and tool catalog cache identities, and avoid reading host environment values for executor-only identities.

## Testing

Add regression coverage for legacy executors, cached declarations after a capability downgrade, policy preservation through catalog rebuilds, and connection and tool cache isolation.
